stories.title: Is a New Nuclear Arms Race Already Here?
alternates: The US, Russia and China: is the nuclear build-up real?
What the warhead counters say about a new nuclear arms race
stories.question: Is a new nuclear arms race really starting between the US, Russia and China?
stories.whyWatch: The people who count warheads now call it an arms race, but their own numbers show only one of the three is growing its stockpile today; the gap between the label and the count is the story.
stories.tension: SIPRI and the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists say arms-race dynamics are back and the post-Cold War fall in warheads is set to reverse, yet US and Russian stockpiles held steady in 2025 and the expansion so far is China's.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Year-on-year warhead and deployment counts for the US and Russia after New START expired, showing whether the forecast rise has begun.
gaps: odni-annual-threat-assessment-2026.txt differs: US intelligence describes Russia and China modernizing and expanding nuclear forces built to penetrate US missile defences, consistent with intensifying competition, though it does not call it an arms race.

bulletin-doomsday-clock-2026-disruptive-technologies.txt differs: The Bulletin describes growing belligerence among the US, Russia and China in space and a deepening arms race driven by missile defence, with Russia and China contemplating nuclear weapons in space; it shows a strategic arms race, not specifically a race in nuclear arsenals.

dod-china-military-power-report-2025.txt differs: DoD shows China's side of it (heading for 1,000+ warheads by 2030 to achieve 'strategic counterbalance' with the US), but says nothing here about US or Russian build-ups.

sipri-ai-nuclear-nexus-governance-2025.txt differs: SIPRI says nearly all nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, driven in large part by emerging technologies such as AI, which supports a competitive build-up but does not establish a US-Russia-China arms race as such.

fri-xpt-forecasting-existential-risks-2023.txt differs: XPT superforecasters expected warhead numbers to rise (13,500 by 2040 from 12,705) while nuclear experts expected a fall to 11,990, so forecasters split on a renewed build-up.
stories.premise: Two expert bodies judge it an arms race: the Bulletin calls major-power competition 'a full-blown arms race', and SIPRI says the decades-long decline in warhead numbers is likely to reverse as dismantlement slows and new deployments accelerate. The limits matter. The growth in warhead numbers so far is China's (the DoD expects over 1,000 by 2030); for the US and Russia the evidence is modernization of delivery systems and a forecast rise, not yet bigger stockpiles. US intelligence describes the same modernizing and expanding forces without calling it an arms race, part of the Bulletin's case is about missile defence and space rather than warheads, and forecasters split: superforecasters expected global warhead numbers to rise, nuclear experts expected a fall.

arc.hook: With New START gone, is a three-way nuclear arms race starting?
arc.conflict: The watchdogs say yes; the stockpile counts for the US and Russia have not moved yet.
arc.evidence: SIPRI's reversal forecast and the Bulletin's 'full-blown arms race' judgment, against China's measured growth, US and Russian modernization, the ODNI's more cautious description and the split forecasts.
arc.resolution: The competition is real and building, with China growing now and the US and Russia modernizing; calling it a race in numbers on all three sides is a forecast, not yet a measurement.
arc.takeaway: An arms race in the making: judged by experts, measured so far mainly in China, and expected rather than observed for the US and Russia.

coherence.explanation: One claim, one question: is a three-way nuclear build-up under way, judged by the bodies that count warheads.

stories.question: Is it true that the US and China are headed for war?
stories.whyWatch: Two confident, opposite answers to the same question. Explaining why they differ (population, task, timing, design) teaches more than either headline.
stories.tension: The sources split: metaculus-us-china-war-before-2035.txt says wrong, fri-nuclear-risk-expert-forecasts-2024.txt says wrong, ddis-intelligence-outlook-2025.txt says partly, eurasia-group-top-risks-2026.txt says wrong, hanania-2021-thucydides-trap-myth-ssq.txt says wrong, atlantic-council-global-foresight-2036.txt says partly.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The studies on each side compared on design, population and timing, to explain the split rather than pick a winner.
gaps: Reviewer: The question is a forecast of an event that has not happened, so no study can decide it. Every source is a forecast or a reading of history: Metaculus (wrong, 0.4: 8.7% before 2035), the FRI expert panel (0.35), Eurasia Group (0.3), DDIS (partly, 0.35: both sides preparing for a confrontation neither wants), the Atlantic Council strategist survey (partly, 0.25) and Hanania on the Thucydides-trap base rate (0.3); further expert surveys and superforecaster panels (CFR Preventive Priorities, the 2021 UnHerd superforecaster panel on Taiwan) are the same kind of evidence and would not reach 0.5. stories.title: Could a War With Iran Become World War 3?
alternates: Iran, Russia and China: how close did the 2026 war come to a world war?
Would Russia and China fight for Iran?
stories.question: Could a war with Iran turn into World War 3?
stories.whyWatch: The fear that an Iran war drags in Russia and China was tested in 2026: the war came to the brink of a wider regional war, and what Moscow and Beijing actually did is on the record.
stories.tension: Commentators warned an attack on Iran could spark a world war; in the 2026 war the fighting stayed regional and Russia and China backed Iran with UN vetoes, not forces.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Evidence on whether any great power beyond the US entered or prepared to enter the fighting, and assessments of Russian and Chinese willingness to defend Iran militarily in a future war.
gaps: No study strong enough to decide: "A US or Israeli war with Iran could escalate into a wider world war"
stories.premise: Two claims decide it. Would the war widen into a world war? The evidence supports regional, not world, escalation: the Doha Institute says forty days of fighting brought the region to the brink of a wider war and an energy crisis before a ceasefire, and PRIO says the Middle East escalation raises the risk of a large multi-country regional conflict; no study shows a path to a world war. Would Russia and China fight for Iran? In 2026 they did not: they vetoed a Security Council resolution on Hormuz and stayed out of the fighting. Estonian intelligence (EFIS) says Moscow tends to forget its allies in times of need, and the Pentagon judges Beijing reluctant to deepen its modest defence ties with Iran. The limits: that is one war and two separate judgments, one about Russia and one about China, not a guarantee for every future war; and no study puts a probability on a world war starting from Iran.

arc.hook: When the US and Israel went to war with Iran, people asked whether this was the start of World War 3.
arc.conflict: A world war needs great powers to join; the warnings assumed Russia and China would.
arc.evidence: The 2026 war reached the brink of a wider regional war, but Russia and China acted only at the UN; EFIS on Russia and the DoD on China explain why; PRIO frames the risk as regional.
arc.resolution: The evidence shows a real risk of a wider Middle East war and no sign of a world war: in 2026 Russia and China did not fight for Iran. That is the record of one war and analysts' judgments, not proof they never would.
arc.takeaway: Watch whether outside great powers commit forces; without that, an Iran war is a regional war, however dangerous.

stories.question: Is it really true that russia is winning the war in Ukraine [2026]?

stories.question: Why do studies disagree about whether A Chinese invasion of Taiwan would most likely fail at great cost to all sides?
stories.whyWatch: Two confident, opposite answers to the same question. Explaining why they differ (population, task, timing, design) teaches more than either headline.
stories.tension: The studies split: csis-first-battle-of-the-next-war-2023.txt says right, odni-annual-threat-assessment-2026.txt says partly, metaculus-china-full-scale-invasion-of-taiwan.txt says wrong.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The studies on each side compared on design, population and timing, to explain the split rather than pick a winner.
gaps: What explains the split between csis-first-battle-of-the-next-war-2023.txt, odni-annual-threat-assessment-2026.txt, metaculus-china-full-scale-invasion-of-taiwan.txt?

odni-annual-threat-assessment-2026.txt: US intelligence reports Chinese officials recognise an amphibious invasion would be extremely challenging with a high risk of failure, especially if the US intervened; it does not say failure is most likely.
stories.premise: The studies split on "A Chinese invasion of Taiwan would most likely fail at great cost to all sides": csis-first-battle-of-the-next-war-2023.txt says right, odni-annual-threat-assessment-2026.txt says partly, metaculus-china-full-scale-invasion-of-taiwan.txt says wrong.
